pinterest.title: Korean Traditional Wedding Customs: The Ham, the Ceremony and the Pyebaek, Step by Step
pinterest.description: A Korean traditional wedding is rarely a single ceremony. It is a sequence: a gift box carried to the bride's family, gifts passed between two households, a ceremony, then a quieter room, the pyebaek, where the couple bow to the groom's family. Our guide walks through each Korean wedding tradition in the order many families live them today, for couples marrying in South Korea or bringing the customs home to Australia.

pinterest.title: The Pyebaek: Bows, Rice Wine and Catching Jujubes and Chestnuts at a Korean Wedding
pinterest.description: At many Korean weddings, the couple change into hanbok for the pyebaek. They make a deep, formal bow to the groom's parents, who offer rice wine and words of advice. Near the end, the parents toss jujubes and chestnuts and the couple try to catch them in the bride's wide skirt, then the groom carries the bride on his back around the room. Many Korean-Australian couples hold a pyebaek at home after a Western ceremony.

pinterest.title: Korean Wedding Ducks: The Wooden Wedding Geese of a Traditional Korean Wedding
pinterest.description: In a traditional Korean wedding, the groom brings wooden geese to the bride's family in a ritual called jeonallye. Geese are a symbol of loyalty and fidelity, and the pair was given as a sign of the groom's everlasting love for his bride. Today the geese often sit on the ceremony table wrapped in cloth, and couples take them home and keep them on display. If you are marrying away from Korea, ask whether a pair has been handed down in the family.

slides: A Korean traditional wedding is not one ceremony. It is a sequence.
The ham: before the wedding, the groom's family sends a wrapped box of gifts to the bride's family, tied in cloth for the journey.
Yedan and yemul: gifts pass between the two households. Many couples now scale them down, so talk early.
The wedding hall: many couples hold a brisk Western-style ceremony, then change into hanbok for the pyebaek.
The jeontong honrye: in the full traditional ceremony, the couple bow to each other and share a cup across a ceremony table.
The wooden wedding geese, often called Korean wedding ducks, are a symbol of loyalty and fidelity.
The pyebaek: the couple bow to the groom's parents and try to catch jujubes and chestnuts in the bride's skirt.

instagram_carousel.caption:
A Korean traditional wedding is rarely a single ceremony. A gift box is carried to the bride's family, gifts pass between two households, the couple marry, and then comes a quieter room: the pyebaek.

At many Korean weddings today, the ceremony takes place in a wedding hall, with a white gown, a suit and a brisk service. Then the couple change into hanbok, and the groom's parents sit behind a low table set with dried fruit, sweets and rice wine. The couple make a deep, formal bow, receive rice wine and advice, and try to catch jujubes and chestnuts in the bride's wide skirt. At many pyebaek, the groom then carries the bride on his back around the room while the family cheers him on.

In the full traditional ceremony, the jeontong honrye, the groom presents wooden wedding geese, often called Korean wedding ducks, to the bride's family. Geese are a symbol of loyalty and fidelity. The bride wears a wonsam or hwarot with a jokduri headpiece, and the groom wears samogwandae.

Customs vary by family, region and faith. The best first step is a simple one: ask both families which parts matter to them.

Our guide walks through each custom in order, then what Australian couples need to know to marry in South Korea or hold a pyebaek at home in Australia.
